raw_text:
Great. Here’s a structured 12-week, bodyweight-friendly strength program for a 27-year-old male beginner training in a small flat with a yoga mat and a doorway pull-up bar. The plan emphasizes progressive overload, safe progressions, and practical progression options you can apply in a confined space. It includes weekly structure, exercises, sets/reps, progression cues, and basic nutrition/recovery guidance.

Assumptions and goals
- Goals: increase overall strength, build muscle, improve movement quality, and establish consistency.
- Equipment: yoga mat, doorway pull-up bar. No additional weights.
- Schedule: 3 non-consecutive strength days per week (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri or Tue/Thu/Sat) with optional 4th mobility/conditioning day on weekends.
- Warm-up: 5–10 minutes dynamic mobility and light activation before each session.
- Progression principle: linear progression in many weeks, with periodic deloads and more challenging progressions every few weeks. If you stall, switch to harder variation rather than increasing volume indiscriminately.

Programming overview
- Phases: 4 phases, each 3 weeks, with a deload in transition between phases (the deload is Week 3 of Phase 3, and Week 1 of Phase 4 is lighter if needed). For clarity:
  - Phase A (Weeks 1–3): Foundational strength and technique. Moderate reps, emphasis on perfect form.
  - Phase B (Weeks 4–6): Progressive overload with increased sets/reps and harder variations.
  - Phase C (Weeks 7–9): Volume and intensity peak; introduce Advanced Bodyweight Variations.
  - Phase D (Weeks 10–12): Consolidation and peaking; deload week if needed, then final strength push.
- Weekly structure: Each week has 3 full-body workouts (A, B, C). Each workout includes Squat/Mandatory lower body, Push, Pull, Core/anti-extension, and Mobility/conditioning as appropriate.
- Sets/Reps targets:
  - Weeks 1–3: 3–4 sets per exercise, 6–12 reps, depending on exercise, with effort aiming at near-failure on last rep of final set.
  - Weeks 4–6: 4 sets, 6–10 reps, with progressive overload (better reps or slightly more difficulty).
  - Weeks 7–9: 4–5 sets, 5–9 reps for main lifts; introduce more challenging variations.
  - Weeks 10–12: 4–5 sets, 5–8 reps; aiming for stronger, controlled reps; finalize with a light deload if needed.

Workout templates you can rotate
- Pull-up progressions are key and can be adapted to a doorway pull-up bar.
- Core work uses time-based holds and carries that don’t require extra equipment.

Phase A: Weeks 1–3 — Foundational strength and technique
Focus: perfect form, establish baseline, light-to-moderate volume.

Workout A
- Goblet-like squat substitute: Bodyweight Squat to a chair or low depth (or supported by a strap around the bar if needed)
  - 3–4 sets x 8–12 reps
- Push-up progressions: Wall push-ups progressing to incline push-ups on a chair, then standard kneeling if capable
  - 3–4 sets x 6–12 reps
- Inverted row progression: Under-doorway row using a towel or bar if available, or “bodyweight row” under a sturdy table (if safe)
  - 3–4 sets x 6–10 reps
- Hip hinge: Glute bridge or hip thrust on mat
  - 3–4 sets x 8–12 reps
- Plank variations: Front plank
  - 3 sets of 20–40 seconds
- Mobility/activation: hip flexor stretch, thoracic spine mobility, scapular wall slides
  - 5–8 minutes

Workout B
- Bulgarian split squat (using chair as support) or step-up progression
  - 3–4 sets x 8–12 reps per leg
- Push-up variant: Elevated push-ups (hands on box/chair) or standard push-ups if able
  - 3–4 sets x 6–12 reps
- Pull-up progression: Dead hang, assisted pull-ups with stabilizing knees tucked or band-like if available; if no band, do negative pull-ups
  - 3–4 sets x 4–6 reps (or 3–5 negatives)
- Hip hinge: Hip thrust on mat or single-leg deadlift progression (bodyweight)
  - 3–4 sets x 8–12 reps
- Side plank: 2–3 sets per side
  - 3 sets x 20–30 seconds
- Mobility/activation: ankle mobility, thoracic rotation
  - 5–8 minutes

Workout C
- Wall sit or chair squat hold: build quad endurance
  - 3–4 sets x 20–40 seconds
- Push-up progressions: continue incline or floor push-ups, focus on tempo
  - 3–4 sets x 6–12 reps
- Pull-up progressions: same as A/B progression, aim for additional reps
  - 3–4 sets x 4–6 reps
- Glute bridge or hinge focus: 3–4 sets x 8–12 reps
- Anti-extension core: dead bug or bird-dog
  - 3 sets x 8–12 reps per side
- Mobility: hips, shoulders
  - 5–8 minutes

Progression cues for Phase A
- Add reps first, then reduce tempo to increase time under tension.
- If you can complete the top end of the rep range with solid form for all sets, progress to a harder variation (e.g., incline to standard push-up, chair squat to deep squat, assisted pull-up to unassisted, etc.).

Phase B: Weeks 4–6 — Progressive overload and technique refinement
Focus: increasing volume and difficulty, introduce more challenging variations while maintaining form.

Workout A
- Squat progression: Split-squat or deep bodyweight squat with tempo (3 seconds down, 1 second hold, 1 second up)
  - 4 sets x 8–12 reps
- Push-up progression: Standard push-ups with tempo (3 seconds down, 1 second hold, explode up)
  - 4 sets x 6–10 reps
- Pull-up progression: Assisted pull-ups or weighted negative reps
  - 4 sets x 4–6 reps
- Hip hinge: Glute bridge march or hip thrust with pause
  - 4 sets x 8–12 reps
- Core: Half-kneeling pallof press is hard without equipment; alternative: dead bug with slower tempo
  - 3 sets x 8–12 reps per side

Workout B
- Lunges or step-ups: Forward step or reverse lunge
  - 4 sets x 8–12 reps per leg
- Push-up progression: Incline to floor push-ups
  - 4 sets x 6–10 reps
- Pull-ups: Increase hold time on top or add negative reps
  - 4 sets x 4–6 reps
- Glute ham raise alternative: Nordic hamstring progression (eccentric) with partner or chair support
  - 3–4 sets x 6–8 reps
- Core: Side plank with knee down or elevated leg
  - 3 sets x 20–30 seconds per side

Workout C
- Pistol squat progression: assisted pistol squat to box
  - 3–4 sets x 6–10 reps per leg (use chair support as needed)
- Push-up progression: Decline push-ups (feet on chair) if possible
  - 4 sets x 6–10 reps
- Pull-up progression: Full range unassisted where possible
  - 4 sets x 4–6 reps
- Hip hinge: Hip thrust with paused hold
  - 4 sets x 8–12 reps
- Core: Bicycle crunch or hollow-body hold
  - 3 sets x 20–30 seconds

Phase C: Weeks 7–9 — Volume and intensity peak with advanced bodyweight variations
Focus: higher effort, more demanding positions, maintain good technique.

Workout A
- Deep squat with tempo: 4 sets x 6–10 reps
- Push-up variants: Diamond push-ups or decline as able
  - 4 sets x 6–10 reps
- Pull-up: Weighted negative or lactate-lactic: add 1–2 more reps
  - 4 sets x 5–8 reps
- Hip extension: Single-leg glute bridge
  - 4 sets x 8–12 reps per leg
- Core: Hanging leg raises substitute with tuck holds on bar if possible
  - 3–4 sets x 6–10 reps or 15–30 seconds hold

Workout B
- Bulgarian split squat with pause at bottom
  - 4 sets x 8–12 reps per leg
- Push-up: Tempo push-ups
  - 4 sets x 6–10 reps
- Pull-up: High-rep set near failure if capable
  - 4 sets x 6–8 reps
- Hip hinge: Skater deadlift with balance
  - 4 sets x 8–12 reps
- Core: Oblique crunches or side plank with reach-through
  - 3 sets x 10–12 reps per side

Workout C
- Pistol squat progressions: to box or supported pistol progression
  - 4 sets x 6–10 reps per leg
- Push-up: Elevated feet to increase difficulty
  - 4 sets x 6–10 reps
- Pull-up: Mixed grip or slow eccentric
  - 4 sets x 5–8 reps
- Glute bridge variations: Hip thrust with single-leg
  - 4 sets x 8–12 reps per leg
- Core: V-ups or dragon flag progression variants (simplified)
  - 3 sets x 8–12 reps

Phase D: Weeks 10–12 — Consolidation and peaking
Focus: solidify gains, bring up weakest lift, ensure consistency, test readiness.

Week 10–11 (load-dense days)
- Maintain 4 sets per main lift with 5–8 reps, focusing on explosive movement where possible (clap push-ups if capable, explosive pull-ups, etc., only if safe)
- Include similar volume to Phase C but slightly lower reps to peak.

Week 12 — Testing and deload
- Re-test: 1RM-like estimates for push-ups, pull-ups (max reps in a set), squats (deep squat depth), and core holds.
- Deload: If fatigued, reduce volume by roughly 40–50% and maintain technique.

General guidelines for all weeks
- Frequency: 3 strength sessions per week, with at least one rest day between sessions.
- Progression:
  - Primary progression: increase reps within the target range while maintaining good form.
  - Secondary progression: move to more challenging variation when you can complete the upper end of the rep range with good form across all sets.
  - When a weekly target becomes difficult, switch to an easier variation for a couple of sets to maintain technique and avoid injury.
- Rest between sets: 60–90 seconds for hypertrophy-focused sets; 2–3 minutes for heavier strength sets if needed (especially for pull-ups and pistol progressions). For beginner, aim 1–2 minutes between sets initially, then lengthen as you approach more challenging sets.
- Tempo: Emphasize control with a 2–0–2 tempo for most exercises (2 seconds down, 0 pause, 2 seconds up). For push-ups and squats, use a slower lowering phase (3 seconds) and controlled ascent (1–2 seconds).
- Technique: Prioritize perfect form over heavier reps. If unsure, reduce range of motion to ensure stability and alignment.

Nutrition and recovery guidance
- Calorie balance: Aim for a slight surplus if the goal is strength and muscle gain, around 250–500 extra calories per day, depending on body size and appetite. If your client struggles with appetite, start with a modest surplus (100–200 calories) and adjust.
- Protein intake: Target 1.6–2.0 g per kg of body weight per day. If hard to achieve, spread protein intake evenly across meals and include a protein source in every meal.
- Hydration: 2–3 liters per day, adjust for activity and environment.
- Sleep: 7–9 hours per night. Consistent sleep improves recovery and performance.
- Recovery protocols:
  - Post-workout nutrition: within 1–2 hours after training, 20–40 g protein plus carbohydrates (e.g., fruits, yogurt, or a protein shake).
  - Mobility and cooldown: 5–10 minutes of light mobility and static stretching after training, focusing on hips, shoulders, and thoracic spine.
  - Deload week: reduce volume and intensity by about 40–50% every 4–5 weeks or if fatigue signs appear.

Notes and safety
- Bodyweight exercises are scalable to progressions; prioritize technique over volume to prevent injury.
- If any joint pain appears (knees, shoulders, elbows), adjust range of motion, switch to less demanding variations, or take an extra rest day.
- For the doorway pull-up bar, ensure it’s securely mounted. Use proper technique to avoid swinging and jerking on the bar.
- If you’re able to add any micro-loads (heavy backpack, filled water bottles) safely, you can progress some movements by loading on the torso in a controlled way, but focus on perfect form with bodyweight first.

Optional minor equipment substitution ideas
- If a chair is available, you can use it for incline push-ups, supported squats, step-ups, and Bulgarian split squats.
- If a towel is available, you can perform rows by anchoring the towel around the pull-up bar or a door frame for an assisted row variation.

Sample weekly rhythm (repeat for all phases)
- Monday: Strength Day A
- Wednesday: Strength Day B
- Friday: Strength Day C
- Optional Saturday: Mobility/conditioning light day (15–20 minutes) focusing on dynamic flexibility, core stability, and light cardio like brisk walking or cycling if space allows.

Optional weekly progression example (Phase A to Phase B example)
- Week 1: 3 sets of 8–12 reps per exercise
- Week 2: 4 sets of 8–12 reps
- Week 3: 4 sets of 10–12 reps or progress to a harder variation if reps got comfortable
- Week 4: Move to Phase B with 4 sets of 6–10 reps and slightly tougher variations

Testing and assessment
- At the end of Week 12, re-test max reps or time for:
  - Push-ups
  - Pull-ups (assisted or unassisted as capable)
  - Bodyweight squats (deep depth)
  - Core holds (plank duration)
- Compare to Week 1 results to gauge progress.

If you want, I can tailor this further to his exact bodyweight, current strength measurements, and any specific target lifts or exercises you’d like to emphasize, and I can lay out a concrete week-by-week table with exact exercise names, reps, and progression milestones.
